scope: These are cultural reading notes, not a taxonomy of people. The dialogues are original fiction: each character has a partial perspective and no character speaks for an entire community. The fictional 1967 feud is not actual LGBTQ history. The notes below distinguish what was inspected from what was not.

sources.title: Black lesbian gender and sexual culture: celebration and resistance
sources.author: Bianca D. M. Wilson
sources.scope: Abstract only; full article not inspected for this revision.
sources.note: Wilson’s qualitative study describes gender and sexual roles in one African American lesbian community as sources of both expectations and resistance. That situated finding cautions against treating a character’s label as a universal rule about behavior, desire or power.

sources.title: Brown Boi Project — About Us
sources.author: Brown Boi Project
sources.scope: Organizational self-description and participant testimony on the About Us page.
sources.note: The organization describes work among masculine-of-center women and queer and trans people of color across racial and gender justice. Its account helps frame masculinity as something people can enjoy, examine and change without assuming identical experiences or power.

sources.title: The Combahee River Collective Statement
sources.author: Combahee River Collective
sources.scope: Selected sections of the primary statement, especially pages 1–4 of this reproduction.
sources.note: The collective connects race, gender, sexuality and class, and pairs solidarity with criticism of sexism. Its position informs the distinction between cooperation and erasure of internal conflict. It is a specific 1977 political statement; it is not evidence for the invented 1967 feud.

sources.title: Stone Butch Blues — selected author notes
sources.author: Leslie Feinberg
sources.scope: Selected author notes, printed pages 333–335 / PDF pages 350–352. No fresh full reading of the novel is claimed.
sources.note: These notes emphasize context, changing terminology, self-definition and collective connection. They provide a reason to let different generations use language differently, rather than force every fictional person into a single present-day vocabulary. The novel’s scenes and prose are not reproduced.

sources.title: What Is a Stud? The History of Black Lesbian Masculinity
sources.author: Them
sources.scope: Brief use of first-person interviews with Cortney Matthewis and $leazy EZ; no interview quotations reused.
sources.note: The interviewees describe varied personal expressions of stud identity, including nonbinary experience, within Black queer culture. These accounts resist a checklist of clothes, sexual roles or personality traits. The fictional Rae speaks for herself.

sources.title: The Gender of Desire: Joan Nestle’s Last Interview — Our Dyke Histories
sources.author: Joan Nestle; interviewer Jack Gieseking
sources.scope: Selected written interview/transcript passages; audio not auditioned.
sources.note: Nestle’s first-person account brings pleasure, class, race and risk into the same social world. It helps foreground femme desire and agency, rather than making a femme character a passive partner or a reward. No interview scene or erotic passage is adapted.

sources.title: Mabel Hampton Oral History Project — Reflections on Lesbian Fashion
sources.author: Lesbian Herstory Archives / Pratt curated exhibit
sources.scope: Curatorial descriptions inspected; recordings not auditioned and no new transcript made.
sources.note: The exhibit’s presentation of Hampton helps check against erasing Black butch lives or equating butchness with whiteness. Clothing and self-description belong to a particular life. June is an invented character, not a portrait of Hampton.

sources.title: Sylvia Rivera’s 1973 speech — transcript in Document Set 3
sources.author: Sylvia Rivera; reproduction by TeachRock
sources.scope: Speech transcript on PDF page 2. The packet’s Stonewall biographical claim is not relied upon.
sources.note: Rivera’s speech challenges exclusion within a movement and asks who provides material support to vulnerable community members. It informs the coalition’s concern with paid work, resources and accountability. Rivera does not appear in the fiction, and no speech is assigned to a fictional character.
